Accordingly, we hold that the interpretation of the word “inventory” in this case is an issue for the judge, not the jury, and affirm

the decision of the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit.
It is so ordered.
NOTES AND QUESTIONS
1.The classic discussion of whether the jury or judge decides if injurious conduct is negligent appears in Holmes, The Common Law 123–26
(1881). See also Gergen, The Jury’s Role in Deciding Normative Issues in the American Common Law, 68 Fordham L.Rev. 407 (1999). How does
Markman affect the assignment of decision-making in the following situations:
(a)In a suit for breach of an oral agreement to clear timber from defendant’s lands, sell it, and pay a set amount of money to defendant,
should the judge or jury determine whether the oral agreement was enforceable under the state Statute of Frauds? If the contract was
interpreted as one for services, it would be enforceable; if it was found to be a contract for the sale of timber, recovery would be
barred. See Dobson v. Masonite Corp., 359 F.2d 921 (5th Cir. 1966) (assigned to jury on a special interrogatory).
(b)In a suit for breach of contract, should the judge or jury determine whether a series of letters that appeared to be contradictory
constituted a contract? See Rankin v. Fidelity Insurance Trust & Safe Deposit Co., 189 U.S. 242, 23 S.Ct. 553, 47 L.Ed. 792 (1903)
(assigned to jury, subject to court’s instructions).
(c)In a suit for breach of contract, should the judge or jury determine whether a letter was written in unambiguous terms? See Holtman
v. Butterfiled, 51 Cal.App. 89, 196 P. 85 (1st Dist.1921) (court).
2. When an issue is classified as one of “law,” the rule binds litigants in subsequent cases. When is the need for a precise legal standard sufficient
to justify withdrawing the matter from the jury? Consider the question whether a posting on the Internet is obscene. Should the decision to give the
question of obscenity to the judge or jury depend on the need for legal certainty, or should consideration also be given to the desirability of informing
the judgment with community values as reflected by several juries in different locales passing on the question? Compare Solomon, The Political Puzzle
of the Civil Jury, 61 Emory L.J. 1331 (2012), with Miller, The Pretrial Rush to Judgment: Are the “Litigation Explosion,” “Liability Crisis,” and
Efficiency Clichés Eroding Our Day in Court and Jury Trial Commitments?, 78 N.Y.U.L.Rev. 982, 1094–1126 (2003).
